questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The catch turned the error into null, an ordinary value. Nothing was thrown, so a caller that does not check the value carries on as if the charge worked. That is swallowing.

questions.q: A card is declined for insufficient funds. What kind of failure is that?
questions.explain: Declines are a normal part of payments. The program has a planned path for them. Retrying would fail again and may annoy the bank.
options: A bug: the code should have prevented it
An expected outcome: tell the customer precisely and let them choose another card
A reason to restart the server

questions.q: Code throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'total') in the checkout. What should the program do?
questions.explain: A bug means the code's assumptions are wrong, so any recovery code is guessing. Recovering with 0 would charge nothing and confirm the order. Fail loudly and fix it.
options: Catch it and use a total of 0
Fail the request with a generic error, log everything, and fix the code: it is a bug
Show the TypeError message to the customer

questions.q: A request to a shipping provider times out. How should it be classified?
questions.explain: The network and other services fail for reasons outside your code. Whether you can recover depends on whether a retry is safe and whether a fallback is acceptable.
options: An expected outcome, shown to the customer as "shipping refused"
An environment failure: possibly recoverable by retrying (if the operation is idempotent) or by failing cleanly

questions.q: A kindOf(error) helper sees an error that is not one of the app's own classes. What should it return by default?
questions.explain: Unknown errors must be treated as the most serious kind. Showing their message can leak internals; retrying them can repeat damage.
options: "expected", so the customer sees the message
"bug", so it is not shown to users or retried blindly
Nothing; unknown errors should be ignored

questions.q: A function calls something that can throw. Which is not one of the three honest choices?
questions.explain: Logging and returning a default is swallowing: the caller continues on a false assumption. Letting the error pass is the most common correct choice.
options: Handle it, if the function knows a correct way to continue
Translate it into an error that means something at this level, keeping the original as cause
Let it pass up to a caller
Log it and return a default value so the caller does not have to care

questions.q: How many log lines does one failure produce?
questions.explain: Each layer logged and re-threw, so one failure became three log lines. Log once, where the error is handled (here the handler); the other try/catch blocks add nothing.

questions.q: In a layered service, where should an error be logged?
questions.explain: One failure should be one log entry. Intermediate layers add information by translating the error with cause, not by writing extra log lines.
options: In every function it passes through, to be safe
Only in the function that threw it
Once, at the boundary that handles it, with the full cause chain and a request id

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each wrapper keeps the error below it in cause. Following the links goes from the business-level message down to the root detail.

questions.q: A layer wraps an error. What does this print?
questions.explain: The wrapper forgot { cause: error }, so the original SyntaxError is gone and nobody can tell what was wrong with the data. Always pass the cause when translating.

questions.q: Where is wrapping an error with cause most useful?
questions.explain: A link in the chain should add meaning. Wrapping in every function adds links that repeat the same information.
options: In every function, so the chain is as long as possible
At boundaries where the vocabulary changes, such as network to gateway, or gateway to payment
Never; the stack trace is enough

questions.q: A retry loop decides whether to retry. Which check is most robust?
questions.explain: Messages are for people and get reworded. Decisions should read machine-readable facts that the error's designer put there on purpose.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Error.isError checks for a genuine error object (even from another realm), not for something shaped like one. Strings and look-alike objects are not errors.
questions.code:
const fake = { name: "Error", message: "not really", stack: "" };
console.log(Error.isError(new RangeError("x")), Error.isError(fake), Error.isError("boom"));

questions.q: A library does throw "insufficient funds". What should your code do where it calls that library?
questions.explain: Code above that point assumes errors have a message and a stack. Normalising at the edge where foreign code is called keeps that assumption true.
options: Normalise: wrap non-errors in a real Error (keeping the value as cause) so the rest of the code can rely on name, message and stack
Convert the string to a number
Ignore it, because it is not an error

questions.q: Which situation is the best fit for AggregateError?
questions.explain: AggregateError is for several independent failures reported together. One failure with a history is a cause chain.
options: A network error that caused a gateway error that caused a payment error
Three independent invalid fields on a signup form that the user should see together

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first argument is the list, stored in .errors; the second is the message. Each inner error keeps its own type and fields.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.any succeeds with the first fulfilled promise. When every one rejects, it rejects with an AggregateError whose .errors holds each reason.

questions.q: A nightly job pays 50 vendors. Two payouts fail. What should the job report?
questions.explain: Independent operations should not stop each other, and a partial success must be recorded so the retry only covers what failed.
options: Only the first failure, then stop
Nothing: 48 succeeded, so the job succeeded
Which vendors were paid and an AggregateError with both failures, so a retry does not pay anyone twice and nothing is lost
Throw a generic "batch failed" and retry all 50

questions.q: When is it safe to retry "charge ₦23,278.50 for ORD-7" after a timeout?
questions.explain: A timeout does not tell you whether the charge happened. With an idempotency key, the gateway returns the existing charge instead of creating a second one, so the retry is safe.
options: When the gateway supports an idempotency key and every attempt sends the same key for the same order
Only if the timeout was shorter than 5 seconds

questions.q: Which idempotency key is correct for charging an order?
questions.explain: The key identifies what you are doing, not which attempt. A new key per attempt would make every retry a new charge.
options: A new random id for each attempt
A key derived from the intent, such as charge:ORD-7, used for every attempt of that charge

questions.q: The card was charged, then saving the order to the database failed. What should the order service do?
questions.explain: Two systems cannot share one transaction, so the program undoes the first step itself. Compensation is cleanup: the request still fails.
options: Return success; the money was taken
Compensate by refunding the charge, then let the failure propagate; if the refund also fails, report both so a person can act
Swallow the error and try saving later without telling anyone

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both the save and the compensation failed, so both errors are reported together. Throwing only the refund error would hide why the refund was attempted.
options: manual action needed | db down, refund window closed

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A return in finally replaces whatever the try block was doing, including a thrown error. Use finally only for cleanup, never for return.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without await, the function returns the promise before it rejects, so the rejection happens outside the try and its own catch never runs: A rejects. return await keeps the rejection inside, so B's catch handles it. B prints first because an async function that returns a promise needs extra microtask steps to adopt that promise's result, while B already had a plain value to return.
options:
B: handled inside
A rejected: save failed

A: handled inside
B: handled inside

A rejected: save failed
B rejected: save failed

A rejected: save failed
B: handled inside

questions.q: Is an empty catch {} ever acceptable?
questions.explain: An empty catch destroys all evidence of a failure. If ignoring is right, make that decision visible to the next reader and to your monitoring.
options: Yes, whenever the error is annoying
Rarely: only when ignoring the failure is truly correct (a best-effort cache write), with a comment explaining why and ideally a metric counting it

questions.q: When is returning a result object ({ ok: false, error }) a better design than throwing?
questions.explain: A result object forces the caller to look at the outcome. Throwing fits failures most callers cannot handle and should pass up. The danger is a failure value that looks like success, such as null.
options: When failure is a normal outcome that every caller must branch on, such as "is this coupon valid?"

questions.q: What is the job of an error boundary in a queue worker?
questions.explain: The unit of work is one job. A bug in job 2 must not stop jobs 3 to 1,000, and it must not disappear either.
options: To catch any error from one job, log it once, mark that job failed or retry it, and keep processing the other jobs
To stop the worker at the first error
To hide errors from the logs

questions.q: An HTTP boundary catches an error that is not one of the app's own error classes. What should the response contain?
questions.explain: Unexpected errors can reveal file paths, SQL or library versions. Only errors designed for users carry user-facing messages.
options: The error's message and stack, to help the client developer
A generic 500 message; the details go to the logs

questions.q: What should a Node service do in its unhandledRejection handler?
questions.explain: An error that escaped every boundary is a bug, and the process may be in an unknown state. The process boundary is a last-resort safety net, not a place to handle errors.
options: Ignore the rejection and keep serving requests
Log it properly, then shut down cleanly and let a supervisor restart the process
Send the error to the last client that made a request

questions.q: The payment gateway returns status 200 but no id field. How should the gateway client report it?
questions.explain: Something is wrong with the integration, not with the customer's card. Reporting it as a decline misleads the customer; retrying repeats the problem.
options: As a retryable error, so it is tried again
As a plain, non-retryable error describing the unexpected response: it is a contract failure, treated like a bug
Return { id: undefined } and let the order service deal with it

questions.q: Finish loadPrices(text): parse the JSON, and if parsing fails throw an Error with the message price list is corrupt that keeps the original error as its cause.
questions.explain: The new message says what failed at this level; cause keeps the SyntaxError for whoever debugs it.

questions.q: Write rootCause(error) that follows .cause links while the cause is an Error and returns the deepest error.
questions.explain: Walk down the chain until an error has no error as its cause. (A production version also guards against chains that loop, as in the lesson's exercise.)

questions.q: Write validateLines(lines): every line needs a whole-number qty of at least 1. Collect a problem Error with the message SKU: bad quantity QTY for each bad line and throw one AggregateError with the message N lines are invalid. Return the lines if all are valid.
questions.explain: Collect every problem first, then throw once, so the user sees all of them. The inner errors keep their own messages.
questions.expected:
2 lines are invalid
  OIL-1: bad quantity 0
  SALT: bad quantity 1.5
1

questions.q: Write withRetry(task, attempts): call task(); if it throws an error with retryable === true, try again, up to attempts calls in total. Rethrow non-retryable errors immediately, and rethrow the last error when the attempts run out.
questions.explain: Only retryable errors are retried, and only within the budget. A decline stops after one call: retrying it could never succeed.

questions.q: Write runJobs(jobs, handler), a per-job error boundary: run handler(job) for every job, print ok ID or failed ID: MESSAGE, and return { done, failed } counts. One failing job must not stop the others.
questions.explain: The try/catch sits around each unit of work, not around the whole loop, so a bug in job 2 is recorded and job 3 still runs.
questions.expected:
ok 1
failed 2: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'toLowerCase')
ok 3
{ done: 2, failed: 1 }

questions.q: Why is a bug (such as a TypeError from reading a property of undefined) not recoverable by the running program?
questions.explain: A TypeError can be caught, but catching it does not make the program correct. Fail the unit of work, log it, and fix the code.
options: Because the code's own assumptions are wrong, so any recovery code runs on the same wrong assumptions; only changing the code fixes it
Because bugs always crash the process
Because JavaScript has no way to retry

questions.q: The live exchange-rate service is down. When is using a rate cached ten minutes ago an acceptable fallback?
questions.explain: A fallback is a business decision that depends on the use. It must be visible in logs or metrics, never silent.
options: When the business accepts a slightly stale rate for that purpose (showing prices), and the fallback is logged; not when settling a payment that must use the current rate
Only if the cached rate is higher

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: AggregateError takes the same options as Error, including cause, and it is a subclass of Error.
questions.code:
const error = new AggregateError([new Error("a")], "batch failed", { cause: new Error("root") });
console.log(error.errors.length, error.cause.message, error instanceof Error);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The class says "this was designed", the flag says whether trying again can help, and anything else counts as a bug.

questions.q: Write toError(value): return value if it is a real error (use Error.isError), otherwise a new Error with the message non-error thrown: VALUE (the value as JSON) and the value as its cause.
questions.explain: Normalising at the edge means every layer above can rely on name, message and stack, and the original value is still available as cause.
